standard.title: Develop listening and performance skills
standard.description: develop and practise listening/aural skills and vocal and/or instrumental skills/techniques for manipulating elements of music to achieve expressive effects
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can develop listening/aural skills and skills for manipulating elements of music to achieve expressive effects when composing, singing and playing instruments (AC9AMU6D01). They have not yet focused on documenting their developing skills, experimenting with digital tools for arranging, or extending and varying harmonic, rhythmic and melodic patterns systematically.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students develop and practise listening/aural skills and vocal/instrumental techniques for manipulating elements of music to achieve expressive effects, documenting their ideas and progress as a reference for performance and composition.

nodes.label: Listening with intent — aural skill development
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use focused listening to identify how elements of music are being manipulated and how this creates expressive effects
nodes.minimum_width: Listen to a piece and identify at least one expressive effect achieved through manipulation of an element of music (e.g. how dynamic shaping creates tension, how rhythmic articulation creates drive)
nodes.typical_width: Identify multiple expressive effects across a listening example; use music terminology accurately; connect what is heard to specific performance choices
wider: Use a listening diary/journal format to document aural observations across multiple pieces over time — identify patterns in how expressive effects are achieved across different styles
Listen to and compare multiple recordings of the same piece to evaluate how different performers manipulate elements differently to achieve expressive effects

response_modes.reason: Aural identification is a precision skill built through repeated attentive listening. Students need sustained practice connecting what they hear to musical terminology and cause-effect reasoning — breadth of listening material helps, but the cognitive work is the focused listening habit itself.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one expressive effect in a listening example
Connects the effect to a specific manipulation of a musical element

nodes.label: Technical and expressive performance skills
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can practise technical and expressive performance skills including intonation, pitch/rhythmic accuracy, phrasing, dynamics and articulation to communicate expressive intent
nodes.minimum_width: Practise at least one technical or expressive skill (e.g. intonation, phrasing, dynamic control) with a focus on communicating expressive intent; identify what improved and what remains to work on
nodes.typical_width: Practise multiple technical and expressive skills in combination; use deliberate practice strategies to address specific weaknesses; evaluate progress against intended expressive outcomes
wider: Record alternative approaches to interpreting a phrase or melody and evaluate each to identify which best communicates the intended expressive effect — explain what the ear notices that playing alone doesn't reveal
Experiment with different ways to control tone and volume in solo and ensemble contexts — evaluate how balance and blend affect the expressive character of the music

response_modes.reason: Technical and expressive performance skills require deliberate, sustained practice with feedback — this is where the cognitive work is repetitive and iterative by design. Breadth of skills matters, but the learning mechanism is practice-and-evaluate, not exposure to more contexts.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The self-recording and evaluation direction is genuinely rich — students who extend here are developing metacognitive practice habits that transfer across all future performance work. This is a meaningful capability investment beyond minimum.
success_criteria: Practises at least one technical or expressive skill with an identified intent
Can describe what changed through practice and what remains to work on

nodes.label: Extending and varying patterns
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can extend and vary harmonic, rhythmic or melodic patterns, including developing chord progressions and improvising over them
nodes.minimum_width: Take an existing pattern (chord, rhythmic or melodic) and vary or extend it in at least one way; explain the musical effect of the variation
nodes.typical_width: Experiment with multiple ways to vary a pattern (e.g. vary chord ordering to create a progression, vary rhythmic pattern for feel, vary melodic pattern for development); evaluate which variations serve a musical purpose
wider: Identify the qualities of chords in isolation, experiment with different orderings to create chord progressions, then improvise a melody over the progression — evaluate how the progression shapes the melodic possibilities
Investigate how repeating patterns (ostinati) create different effects when layered — compose or improvise additional parts that interact with an established ostinato

response_modes.reason: Students often vary patterns randomly without understanding the musical logic. Encountering pattern variation across harmonic, rhythmic and melodic domains — and hearing what each type of variation does expressively — helps students build a vocabulary of deliberate variation strategies rather than trial-and-error.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The chord quality → progression → improvisation chain is a genuinely rich extended direction — it integrates aural, theoretical and creative skills in a sequence that develops improvisatory capability meaningfully beyond the minimum.
success_criteria: Varies or extends at least one pattern in a deliberate way
Can describe the musical effect of the variation

nodes.label: Using digital tools in practice
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can experiment with digital tools to arrange musical ideas or create effects, using digitally produced parts alone or in combination with voice or acoustic instruments
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least one digital tool to arrange a musical idea or create an effect; describe what the digital tool makes possible that acoustic means alone would not
nodes.typical_width: Experiment with multiple digital tools or approaches; evaluate how digital production choices affect the expressive character of the music; integrate digital and acoustic elements
wider: Use digital tools to create effects (e.g. loops, layering, processing) that combine with acoustic performance — evaluate how the blend affects the stylistic and expressive outcome
Use software to write additional parts (e.g. a bassline to accompany a melody) and evaluate how the added parts change the musical texture and expressive effect

response_modes.reason: Students need hands-on experience with a range of digital tools to understand what each affords — DAWs, notation software, loop-based production and effects processing are distinct tools with different creative possibilities. Accumulating experience across these builds a working digital toolkit.

success_criteria: Uses at least one digital tool to arrange or create a musical effect
Can describe at least one thing the digital tool makes possible or easier

nodes.label: Documenting practice and intentions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can document their musical ideas, practice progress and performance or compositional intentions in a format useful for future reference
nodes.minimum_width: Document musical ideas, rehearsal decisions or expressive intentions in at least one format (written, notation, recording, or digital); the documentation is usable as a reference
nodes.typical_width: Use documentation consistently across practice — notation charts, listening diary entries, transcriptions, recordings — as a working reference that informs and develops their practice
wider: Use a listening diary/journal to document ideas for compositions, interpretations or re-imaginings over time — review entries to identify patterns in their musical thinking and preferences
Write or notate a chart or lead sheet from a songwriting workshop, or transcribe a bassline or additional part — evaluate how the act of documenting clarifies musical thinking

response_modes.reason: Documentation as a practice habit requires repeated reinforcement — students need to experience the feedback loop of documenting → returning to → building on their notes before the habit becomes automatic. Variety of documentation formats matters less than consistency of the practice.

success_criteria: Produces at least one piece of documentation (written, notation, or recording) that captures a musical idea or decision
The documentation is in a format usable for future reference
